title: The towers
hook: Marpa has him build towers and tear them down, again and again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milarepa's revenge, and the remorse that sent him looking for a teacher. Your line was he turned back. Which harm did you set down? Day nine hundred seventy-three.

Milarepa finally finds Marpa, the farmer-translator, plowing a field. He bows and asks for the teaching. He offers himself, body, speech and mind. And Marpa, the great teacher he has wept just to hear named, says something like this: fine, but you can't have food and teaching both. Choose. Milarepa has nothing to offer but his own two hands. So Marpa points to a ridge and gives him a job. Build me a tower. Today: the towers.
screen: `MILAREPA FINDS MARPA.` → `FOOD OR TEACHING: CHOOSE.` → `BUILD ME A TOWER.`

segments.voice: First, the building. Milarepa hauls stones on his back and builds the tower, alone. When it's partly done, Marpa comes to look and says he wasn't thinking clearly when he asked for it. Tear it down, and put every stone back where you found it. Second, again. A new spot, a new shape, a new tower. Again Marpa changes his mind. Again it comes down. The story repeats it, and each time, Milarepa's back grows more raw from the stones, and still no teaching comes. Third, the hidden kindness. Marpa's wife, Dagmema, sees it all and pleads for him. She even helps him with a trick to win some teaching from another student, which Marpa later uncovers. Milarepa despairs and nearly gives up. Fourth, what it was for. In the story, Marpa finally explains. The towers were never about towers. Milarepa had done terrible harm, and the endless labor, borne without anger, was a way to purify it. Marpa's harshness, he says, was itself the teaching. Then, at last, he accepts Milarepa as his student. The story is extreme, and it is about one student with one past; it is no rulebook for how a teacher may treat anyone. What it offers the rest of us is the rhythm: build, take it down, build again, without bitterness. And a look back at the week. Shantideva taught us to exchange self and other. Atisha lit a lamp for the path, and kept a cook for patience. Naropa left his post to serve Tilopa. Marpa walked to India and back. Milarepa turned from harm. Today, he picks up the first stone.
screen: `BUILD IT. TEAR IT DOWN.` · `AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` · `DAGMEMA PLEADS FOR HIM.` · `THE LABOR WAS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `BUILD IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin again, without bitterness. Settle, and breathe. Notice your attention. Sooner or later it will wander off, to a plan, a worry, a sound. When you notice, don't scold it. Just set the stone down where you found it, and come back to the breath, like starting a new tower. Again. And again. Each return is the practice, not a failure of it. The bell holds the time.
The towers. The ones Marpa had Milarepa build and tear down, again and again, as a way to purify his past. Today's word.
Your line: build it again. Today, take one task that went wrong or got undone, and do it again, patiently, with no grumbling. Day nine hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Milarepa's towers as a teaching on purifying past harm and on perseverance, and in the Kagyu tradition a tower in southern Tibet is honored as the one tradition says Milarepa finally completed for Marpa's son.

fork.setup: you're Milarepa. you've built a tower for Marpa, your back is raw, and he tells you to tear it down and put the stones back. what do you do?
options: tear it down and build again.
argue until he admits he's wrong.
fork.reveal: Milarepa tore it down and built again, more than once, before Marpa finally accepted him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cruel teacher playing games.
what it means: in the story, the endless building and unbuilding was how Milarepa purified the harm he had done.
what a scholar hears: the hardship itself named as the teaching, and Marpa's wife Dagmema as the voice of mercy beside it.
recall: the Buddha who is to come
